summary: Identifies the need for DNS extensions to Network Address Translators and outlines how a DNS Application Level Gateway can meet it. It is informational.

eli5.summary: When a house shares one public address, name lookups need translation too. A helper does that.

questions: how does dns work with nat
why do dns addresses change with nat
subtitle: How DNS names map to addresses when NAT hides private networks

tldr.problem: Network Address Translators (NATs) hide internal private addresses and map them to public addresses for the outside world. But DNS name-to-address mappings are embedded in application data. When a DNS query returns an address, the application may not know whether to use the private address (inside) or public address (outside).
tldr.mechanism: A DNS Application Level Gateway (DNS_ALG) sits on the NAT device and intercepts DNS packets. It modifies the DNS payload transparently: outgoing queries change private addresses to public ones, incoming responses change public back to private, based on the NAT's state information.
tldr.outcome: DNS_ALG allows hosts in a NAT network to resolve names correctly whether they are inside the private network or outside. It supports both dynamic address assignment and static mappings, with optional TTL adjustment for dynamic addresses.

facts.label: Core concept
facts.value: DNS Application Level Gateway on NAT devices

today: RFC 2694 is Informational and describes the DNS_ALG architecture for NAT-based networks. While NAT techniques have evolved (including CGNAT and dual-stack), the need to translate DNS responses in NAT environments remains relevant. Modern implementations use similar principles, though some modern protocols try to minimize dependency on DNS address lookups.

sections.title: The DNS and NAT Problem
sections.content:
Network Address Translators (NATs) sit at the boundary of a private network and translate between private IP addresses (internal) and public IP addresses (external). This hides internal addresses from the outside world and lets many internal machines share a single public IP. The NAT modifies the IP and TCP/UDP headers of packets to perform this translation.

However, applications often embed IP addresses in their data, not just in headers. An email application might embed an IP address as the sender's hostname; a web page might contain IP addresses in URLs or server configurations. When these packets cross the NAT, the headers are translated but not the payload, leading to incorrect addresses on the far end.

DNS (Domain Name Service) performs name-to-address mapping. When a host asks What is the IP of example.com?, DNS responds with an address. But which address should be returned—the private address (if the query is from inside) or the public address (if it is from outside)? DNS_ALG solves this by modifying DNS responses based on which side of the NAT the query came from.
sections.eli5: When you email someone from inside your company, you sign as user@192.168.1.5 (internal). But when someone outside receives your email, they see user@98.76.54.3 (public). DNS must give different answers depending on who asks.

sections.title: DMZ and Address Binding
sections.content:
A typical private network has a DMZ (demilitarized zone)—a subnet accessible from both inside and outside, containing web servers, mail servers and DNS name servers. DMZ hosts have both private and public addresses. Internal hosts (behind the DMZ) are only known by private addresses.

The RFC distinguishes two types of address binding. Static address binding means a private address is permanently mapped to the same public address. Dynamic address binding means a private address is assigned a temporary public address, which may change. For dynamic bindings, there are two phases: temporary binding (when a DNS query reserves an address but no session exists yet) and committed binding (when a real session starts using the reserved address). The Bind-holdout timer defines how long a temporary binding is kept alive; if no session starts before the timer expires, the temporary binding is discarded.

This design prevents denial-of-service attacks where an attacker keeps making DNS queries to exhaust public addresses without ever using them.
sections.eli5: Static binding: your internal IP always becomes 98.76.54.3 to the outside. Dynamic binding: you get 98.76.54.3 just for this session, and if you do not connect within a minute, it goes back to the pool. This prevents bullies from hogging all the public addresses.

sections.title: Incoming DNS Queries
sections.content:
When an external host looks up a DMZ host's name, the query reaches the DMZ name server. DNS_ALG intercepts this query and modifies it if needed. For name-to-address queries (looking up an A record, like What is the IP of mail.example.com?), DNS_ALG passes the query unchanged to the internal name server, which returns the private address. DNS_ALG then intercepts the response and replaces the private address with the public address assigned by NAT. If no public address has been assigned, NAT creates a temporary binding.

For address-to-name queries (reverse lookups, like What host is at 98.76.54.3?), DNS_ALG must first check if a binding exists. If it does, it replaces the public address octets (in reverse DNS notation) with the private address octets, then forwards to the internal name server. If no binding exists, DNS_ALG refuses the query (returns RCODE 5, meaning refused due to policy).

For dynamic address assignments, DNS_ALG sets the TTL (Time To Live) to 0 or 1, meaning the response should not be cached. This forces applications to do a fresh DNS lookup every time they need the address, ensuring they always get a current binding.
sections.eli5: An outside app asks What is mail.example.com? DNS_ALG intercepts and asks the inside: What is mail.example.com? The inside says 192.168.1.5. DNS_ALG replies to the outside with 98.76.54.3 instead.

sections.title: DNS Record Types and Outgoing Queries
sections.content:
Different DNS record types require different handling by DNS_ALG. A records (name to address) require address replacement in the RDATA section. PTR records (address to name, in in-addr.arpa domain) require address replacement in the query name. CNAME, MX, NS and SOA records contain host names but not addresses, so no modification is needed. AXFR queries (zone transfers) are problematic for dynamic address assignments and should be restricted to static addresses or not permitted across the NAT boundary at all.

For outgoing queries (when internal hosts query external DNS servers), DNS_ALG generally does not modify the packets, because the queries go to external authoritative servers that do not know about internal addresses. However, with certain NAT modes like twice NAT (where both internal and external networks use overlapping address spaces), DNS_ALG must intercept and modify outgoing queries too.

Dynamic DNS updates should be kept within the same address realm (internal-to-internal) to avoid complexity. If dynamic updates must cross realms, they should use DNSSEC to prevent unauthorized modifications.
sections.eli5: Different DNS record types (A, PTR, MX) contain different information. DNS_ALG is surgical: it only replaces IP addresses where they appear in the specific record type, leaving names and other data alone.

sections.title: Practical Example and Limitations
sections.content:
The RFC walks through a detailed example of DNS_ALG in a bi-directional NAT where a private network 10/8 is mapped to public network 198.76.29/24. When an external host asks for host7 (which has private address 10.0.0.7), DNS_ALG creates a temporary binding to 198.76.29.1, modifies the DNS response to return 198.76.29.1 instead of 10.0.0.7, and sets the Bind-holdout timer. If the external host initiates a session to 198.76.29.1, the temporary binding becomes committed and is kept alive as long as the session exists.

DNS_ALG works transparently for most applications, but has limitations. The modified DNS payload changes length, so IP and TCP/UDP headers and checksums must be updated. Compressed domain names using DNS pointers must have their offsets adjusted. DNS queries on TCP (for zone transfers) must track sequence number deltas to maintain session integrity.

Some configurations require careful planning. For example, if a secondary (backup) DNS name server for a private zone is located outside the NAT, zone transfers with dynamic addresses become impossible—the backup server would receive outdated data, so the RFC recommends keeping both primary and secondary servers within the private domain.
sections.eli5: Say host7 is at 10.0.0.7 inside and 198.76.29.1 outside. An external app queries for host7, gets back 198.76.29.1, connects to it within a minute, and the binding sticks. This works, but DNS is just the first step—the address translation in the packet headers is the actual connection.
